screens.title: KVM and QEMU: Roles and relationship
screens.narratorSegment: KVM and QEMU work together to provide full virtualization on Linux. KVM is the kernel module that exposes hardware virtualization extensions to guests, enabling near-native performance by allowing the guest C P U to run directly on the host C P U when possible. QEMU complements KVM by emulating devices and handling input and output, such as virtual disks, network interfaces, and display devices. Together they form a complete stack: KVM supplies the low-level C P U virtualization, and QEMU supplies machine emulation and device models. A concrete example is a Linux host with Intel VT-x: KVM will create virtual CPUs leveraging VT-x, and QEMU will present a virtual disk in qcow2 format and emulate a network card attached to a libvirt-managed bridge. A common misconception is treating them as interchangeable: they are separate layers — disabling QEMU removes device emulation but not the kernel hypervisor support, while missing KVM prevents hardware acceleration and forces full software emulation with poor performance. Key practice: when validating your virtualization setup, confirm the libvirtd service is running and that qemu-kvm packages are installed. That ensures both layers are present to create performant and fully featured VMs. Takeaway: think of KVM as the fast engine and QEMU as the dashboard and peripherals; both are needed for production virtual machines.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › KVM and QEMU: Roles
Core Concept

KVM vs QEMU

KVM is the kernel hypervisor layer; QEMU emulates devices and handles guest I/O. Both are required for practical virtualization on Linux.

KVM: kernel module
Leverages Intel VT-x or AMD-V to run guest code on host CPU for performance.
QEMU: emulator
Provides device models such as disk, NICs, and virtual graphics for guests.
Why both matter
KVM without QEMU lacks device emulation; QEMU without KVM cannot use hardware acceleration.
Key Takeaway

Both layers are distinct and necessary: confirm packages and libvirtd are active before creating VMs.

Analogy
Think of KVM as the host machine's processor control and QEMU as the set of virtual peripherals and drives the guest can use. One provides the cycles, the other provides what the guest sees.
Concrete example
A host with qemu-kvm installed runs a VM using VT-x acceleration for the CPUs while QEMU presents a qcow2 disk and emulates a virtio network adapter connected to a libvirt bridge. This combination yields near-native CPU performance with flexible device handling.
Common mistake
Assuming KVM is enough. If qemu-kvm packages are missing, device emulation won't be available even if the kernel supports virtualization.
Pro tip
Verify libvirtd is running and that your user is in the libvirt group before attempting VM creation to avoid permission and connection errors.

screens.title: Install and enable libvirt and KVM packages
screens.narratorSegment: Before creating VMs you must install the necessary packages and enable the libvirt daemon. On Red Hat-based distributions, the canonical package set includes qemu-kvm, libvirt-daemon-kvm, libvirt-client, virt-install, and virt-viewer. Installing these packages brings the kernel module, the userland tools, the virt-install command and a graphical viewer for connecting to VMs. After installation, enable and start the libvirtd service so the daemon is active across reboots. Adding your user to the libvirt group removes the need to run virsh with sudo, which makes repeated administration easier and reduces accidental elevated commands. A concrete command sequence is shown in the lab: use dnf to install the packages, systemctl to enable and start libvirtd, and usermod with newgrp to apply group membership without logging out. A common mistake is forgetting to start libvirtd after install or skipping the newgrp step; without the daemon you cannot create or list domains, and without group membership you may get permission errors. After these steps run virsh list --all to confirm libvirt is reachable. That verifies the host is ready for VM creation. Install and enable libvirt and KVM packages means install qemu-kvm, libvirt-daemon-kvm, virt-install, and virt-viewer, enable libvirtd, and add your user to libvirt for permissioned management.. In practical terms, prepare the host so you can create and manage vms. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › Install & Enable
Process

Install packages and start libvirtd

Run the package installation, enable the libvirt daemon, and add your user to the libvirt group. This readies the host to create and manage virtual machines.

sudo dnf install qemu-kvm libvirt-daemon-kvm libvirt-client virt-install virt-viewer -y
sudo systemctl enable --now libvirtd
sudo usermod -aG libvirt $(whoami)
newgrp libvirt
Check
Run virsh list --all. If libvirt is active, virsh will return a list or an empty set rather than a connection error.
Common mistake
Skipping newgrp or relogin leaves you without libvirt group privileges and may cause permission errors when running virsh.
Key Takeaway

Install the packages, ensure libvirtd is running, and add your user to libvirt to allow secure, non-sudo VM management.

Why this matters

A running libvirtd daemon is the host-side control plane for VM lifecycle operations. Without the correct packages and a running daemon, VM creation and management commands will fail.

Example
After installing, enabling libvirtd and adding your user, run virsh list --all to confirm connectivity. If you see an error, check sudo journalctl -u libvirtd for hints.
Misconception
Installing packages alone is not enough; forgetting to enable the daemon is the most frequent reason for "connection refused" errors when using virsh.

screens.title: virt-install command anatomy
screens.narratorSegment: The virt-install command is the primary CLI to define and start virtual machines via libvirt. It accepts options for name, R A M, vCPU count, disk specification, OS variant, network, graphics, installation source, and extra arguments. For example, --name sets the VM identifier used by virsh and the image path; --R A M expects megabytes and --vcpus sets C P U count. The --disk option is flexible: path, size, and format can be set, and qcow2 is a common format because it supports copy-on-write snapshots. Use --os-variant to let virt-install pick tuned defaults for a particular guest operating system. The network option can bind to virbr0 or another bridge, which controls whether the VM is NATed or directly bridged. Graphics may be vnc or spice; for headless installs choose console parameters with --extra-args to enable serial installs. A misconception is that virt-install will always start a graphical console; in many test or server environments you'll want --noautoconsole and to use virt-viewer or virsh console instead. Understanding each flag makes it straightforward to build repeatable, automated VM creation commands for labs and production.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › virt-install Anatomy
Definition

Build a reproducible virt-install command

Each flag maps to an aspect of the VM: compute, storage, network, and installer source. Use explicit options to avoid surprises during automated creation.

--name my-web-server        # VM identifier
--ram 2048                  # memory in MB
--vcpus 2                   # number of virtual CPUs
--disk path=/var/lib/libvirt/images/my-web-server.qcow2,size=20,format=qcow2
--os-variant rhel8.0        # tuned defaults for guest OS
--network bridge=virbr0     # attach to host bridge
--graphics vnc,listen=0.0.0.0
--location /path/to/rhel-8.iso
--extra-args "console=ttyS0,115200n8 serial"
--noautoconsole
Example meaning
The disk option creates a qcow2 image at the path with the requested size; OS variant tunes defaults such as firmware and machine types.
Misconception
Assuming default disk format is raw. Explicitly set format=qcow2 when you want snapshot capability and space savings.
Concrete scenario

If you need a headless server, include the serial extra-args and use --noautoconsole. Later connect with virsh console or virt-viewer if you enabled VNC.

Key Takeaway

Explicit flags make creation repeatable; choose disk format and console options to match your environment and automation needs.

Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › Create VM Example
Code Walkthrough

Sample virt-install command

sudo virt-install \
--name my-web-server \
--ram 2048 \
--vcpus 2 \
--disk path=/var/lib/libvirt/images/my-web-server.qcow2,size=20,format=qcow2 \
--os-variant rhel8.0 \
--network bridge=virbr0 \
--graphics vnc,listen=0.0.0.0 \
--location /path/to/rhel-8.iso \
--extra-args "console=ttyS0,115200n8 serial" \

What to change for tests
Adjust --ram and --vcpus for different workloads, change disk path for LVM-backed storage, or switch --graphics to spice if needed.
Troubleshoot
If installation fails, check that the ISO path is correct and inspect journalctl -u libvirtd for registration errors.
Concrete scenario

Use this command to create a test web server. After install, shut down the VM from within the guest and start it with virsh start my-web-server for lifecycle testing.

Key Takeaway

Use the sample command as a template and modify RAM, vCPUs, disk path, and network to match your environment and automation scripts.

screens.title: Manage VM lifecycle with virsh
screens.narratorSegment: virsh is the essential command-line tool for operating libvirt-managed virtual machines. It is used to list VMs, control their power state, and remove definitions when needed. Commonly used commands include virsh list --all to show all domains, virsh start to power a domain on, and virsh shutdown to request a graceful shutdown using ACPI. When a VM becomes unresponsive you can force power off with virsh destroy, but this is equivalent to unplugging power and can cause data loss. Use virsh suspend and virsh resume to pause and continue a VM's execution, which is useful for short maintenance. Removing a VM's libvirt definition is accomplished with virsh undefine; note that undefine removes the XML definition but leaves disk images on disk unless additional flags are used. For example, a safe recovery workflow is to run virsh destroy only if shutdown fails, then virsh undefine if you intend to re-create a fresh definition while keeping the image for analysis. A misconception is treating destroy as a delete; it does not remove disk files. Always back up disk images before destructive operations. Practice these commands so you can script lifecycle actions reliably during an LFCE exam or in production automation.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › VM Lifecycle with virsh
Process

Common virsh commands

virsh list --all
virsh start my-web-server
virsh shutdown my-web-server
virsh destroy my-web-server   # force off
virsh reboot my-web-server
virsh suspend my-web-server
virsh resume my-web-server
virsh undefine my-web-server
When to use destroy
Only when shutdown fails and you need an immediate power-off. It can cause guest data loss.
Undefine behavior
Undefine removes the VM definition but does not delete disk images by default; this lets you preserve disks for analysis or reuse.
Concrete example

If app-server becomes unresponsive, run virsh destroy app-server to power it off, then run virsh undefine app-server to remove its libvirt entry while keeping the disk image for later analysis.

Common mistake

Do not assume destroy deletes files. Always inspect disk paths before deleting images to avoid data loss.

screens.title: Connect to VMs: virt-viewer and serial console
screens.narratorSegment: Access to a VM can be graphical or serial. virt-viewer provides a graphical window to a VM's console when you create VNC or Spice graphics; it is useful during installations and for desktops. To open a VM's graphical console run virt-viewer followed by the domain name. For headless servers, use a serial console configured via --extra-args in virt-install, which allows virsh console to attach to the guest's serial tty. The serial console is indispensable for servers without a desktop environment and for diagnosing early boot issues like kernel or init failures. A concrete example is adding --extra-args "console=ttyS0,115200n8 serial" to your virt-install command and then connecting with virsh console mytestvm to interact directly with the guest's installation or recovery shell. A common misconception is that virt-viewer or VNC is always available; many production hosts are strictly headless, so planning for serial access avoids being locked out. Always ensure your guest’s bootloader and kernel are configured to output to the serial device when you rely on virsh console. Closing question: which access method will you prioritize for a production headless server and why?

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › Connect to VMs
Definition & Example

virt-viewer and virsh console

Choose virt-viewer for graphical installations and virsh console for headless servers. Configure the serial console during installation for reliable access.

virt-viewer my-web-server
# For serial console, include during install:
--extra-args "console=ttyS0,115200n8 serial"
# Then connect:
virsh console mytestvm
When to use console
Use virsh console for servers without a GUI, for early-boot kernel logs, and when network-based display is not available.
Misconception
Assuming virt-viewer will always succeed. If graphics are not enabled or network policies block VNC, use the serial console instead.
Practical tip

When creating production server images, enable a serial console in the kernel command line so you always have a fallback method to connect for recovery or automation.

Key Takeaway

Plan for console access: configure serial during install and use virt-viewer for graphical needs; this prevents being locked out of VMs.

screens.title: VM storage: qcow2 and best practices
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing a disk format for VM images affects flexibility and operational behavior. qcow2, QEMU's Copy-On-Write format, is popular because it supports snapshots and usually consumes less space than an equivalent raw image due to its thin-provisioning nature. That makes qcow2 ideal for test environments and snapshots during upgrades. However, for high-performance production workloads administrators sometimes prefer block devices on LVM or raw images on dedicated storage to reduce overhead and simplify backup strategies. The virt-install --disk option lets you specify path, size, and format so you can choose qcow2 for flexibility or a raw path for performance. A key practical point is to always back up VM disk images before destructive operations like undefine or manual file deletion. In production, using LVM volumes or dedicated storage backends also helps with snapshot management and integration with storage platform features. A common misconception is that qcow2 is always slower; while there is an overhead compared to raw images, the operational advantages of snapshots and space savings often outweigh that cost for many use cases. Decide based on your workload and backup strategy.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › VM Storage: qcow2
Comparison

qcow2 vs raw / LVM

qcow2 supports copy-on-write snapshots and thin provisioning; raw or LVM-backed disks often give lower overhead and integrate with storage tools for production use.

qcow2
Snapshots, space-efficient, flexible for testing and upgrades.
raw / LVM
Lower overhead and predictable performance for high I/O workloads in production.
Best practice
Back up images before destructive ops; use LVM or dedicated storage for production snapshots and backups.
Key Takeaway

Choose qcow2 for flexibility and snapshots; choose raw or LVM for performance and storage integration in production.

Concrete example

A test VM can be created with a qcow2 disk to quickly snapshot before a risky update. For a database host, place disks on an LVM volume to control placement and performance.

Safety note
Always back up VM disk images before undefine or deletion; undefine removes XML but not the disk unless explicitly requested.

screens.title: Networking: virbr0 and bridge choices
screens.narratorSegment: libvirt typically provides a default virtual network called virbr0 that offers NAT-based connectivity for guests. This is useful for quickly giving VMs outbound network access without manually configuring bridges or host networking. Virbr0 is convenient for labs and for hosts where direct bridged access is not required. However, for production scenarios where a guest needs to be reachable from the same network as the host, administrators create a custom bridge tied to a physical interface and attach the VM directly to that bridge. The virt-install --network bridge=virbr0 flag attaches the VM to the default NAT network; to attach a custom bridge use the bridge name of your choice. A frequent pitfall is expecting virbr0 to provide incoming connections without additional NAT or port-forward rules — it does not expose guest services by default to the broader LAN. For production VMs that must serve traffic directly, plan for a bridged network or configure proper firewall and forwarding rules. Understanding the difference between NAT and bridged networking prevents connectivity surprises after VM provisioning. Networking: virbr0 and bridge choices means virbr0 is a nat bridge for quick outbound networking; create custom bridges for guests that must be directly reachable on the host lan.. In practical terms, understand nat-based virbr0 and when to use custom bridges. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › Networking: virbr0
Architecture

virbr0 vs custom bridge

virbr0 is the default NAT-based bridge created by libvirt to give VMs outbound access. For direct LAN access, attach VMs to a host bridge connected to a physical NIC.

virbr0 (default)
Provides NAT to guests; good for quick labs and isolated testing.
Custom bridge
Connects guests to the host LAN directly for production services reachable by other network hosts.
Pitfall
Assuming virbr0 exposes guest services externally. It does not by default; use a bridged network when external reachability is required.
Concrete example

When creating a VM for testing, --network bridge=virbr0 is fine. For a production VM serving HTTP to other machines on the LAN, create and reference a custom bridge connected to the host interface.

Key Takeaway

Choose virbr0 for quick NATed access; create a bridged interface for services that must be reachable from the network without NAT.

screens.title: Troubleshooting VM creation and runtime issues
screens.narratorSegment: When virt-install or virsh operations fail, start with the error messages and then inspect two reliable sources: virsh dumpxml for the VM's configuration and journalctl -u libvirtd for daemon logs. If virt-install reports an ISO path error, verify that the path exists and is readable by libvirt. If a VM won't start, virsh dumpxml shows disks and network settings that can reveal misconfigured paths or missing devices. The libvirtd journal often contains permission or registration errors from qemu connecting to libvirt. For network failures, confirm your target bridge exists and that the host firewall is not blocking traffic. A recommended safe recovery is to avoid destructive commands until you have a backup: perform virsh shutdown first, then virsh destroy only if shutdown fails, and use virsh undefine only when you explicitly want to remove the definition and understand that disks remain unless you delete them. Always back up disk images before rm or destructive operations. A common misconception is that virsh destroy and undefine delete images; they do not, and administrators should treat disk removal as a separate, intentional step. Following this diagnostic path will minimize downtime and preserve data for analysis.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › Troubleshooting
Process

Diagnose and recover safely

Begin with error messages, then inspect VM XML and libvirt logs. Backup disks before any deletion and use a graceful shutdown before force-off operations.

# Inspect VM configuration
virsh dumpxml my-web-server
# Check libvirt daemon logs
journalctl -u libvirtd
# Confirm bridge exists
ip link show virbr0 || bridge link show
# Safe recovery
virsh shutdown my-web-server
# If shutdown fails
virsh destroy my-web-server
# Remove definition only when ready
virsh undefine my-web-server
Common mistake
Running destructive file removal without confirming disk paths. Use virsh dumpxml to identify image paths first.
Pro tip
If libvirtd reports permission denied, verify group membership, socket permissions, and confirm the service was started after install.
Concrete recovery

If a VM fails to register after virt-install, check the ISO path, run journalctl -u libvirtd to find errors, and inspect virsh dumpxml to confirm the disk and network entries.

Safety note

Back up VM disk images before using destructive commands like rm. Undefine removes the XML only; deletion of disk files is a separate action.

Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › Hands-on Activity
Activity Steps

Create and manage a basic VM

1. Install
Install packages, enable libvirtd, add your user to libvirt, and newgrp libvirt to apply the group change.
2. Download ISO
Place a minimal ISO in /var/lib/libvirt/boot for quick installs.
3. Create VM
Run virt-install with explicit --name, --ram, --vcpus, --disk, --network, and --location options; include --noautoconsole.
4. Connect and install
Use virt-viewer or virsh console to complete the OS installation and then shut down from inside the guest.
5. Manage and clean up
Practice start, shutdown, destroy, and undefine, then remove the disk image only after confirming paths with virsh dumpxml.
Commands to try
virsh list --all
virsh start mytestvm
virsh shutdown mytestvm
virsh undefine mytestvm
sudo rm /var/lib/libvirt/images/mytestvm.qcow2
Key Takeaway

Follow the sequence and verify each step with virsh list and virsh dumpxml; backups before removal are essential.

Third, virsh is the operational tool for listing domains, starting, shutting down, suspending, and undefining VMs; always inspect virsh dumpxml and libvirt logs when troubleshooting. These three points will help you provision, operate, and diagnose VMs effectively during labs and in production. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you will learn how to install and configure the KVM/QEMU virtualization stack and the libvirt management tools, create virtual machines from the command line, and operate them reliably in production. We'll show the concrete commands used to install packages and enable the libvirtd service, walk through a complete virt-install command, and demonstrate how to manage VM lifecycle actions with virsh. You will also learn how to connect to a VM graphically with virt-viewer or by using a serial console, why qcow2 is commonly chosen for VM disks, and how the default virbr0 bridge provides NAT-based networking for quick deployments. A key part of this chapter is practical troubleshooting: reading libvirt daemon logs, inspecting VM XML with virsh dumpxml, and avoiding common mistakes like incorrect ISO paths or disabled libvirtd. By the end, you will be able to provision a minimal VM, bring it up, connect to its console, and diagnose basic failures. Think of this as the essential command-line toolkit for KVM administration — you will practice commands and a short hands-on activity to solidify each step.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to install and configure the KVM/QEMU stack and its management tools, create a virtual machine from the command line using virt-install with specific C P U, memory, disk and network settings, and operate VMs with virsh lifecycle commands. You will also connect to VMs using virt-viewer or the serial console for headless systems, understand the qcow2 disk format and the default virbr0 network bridge, and troubleshoot common failures by inspecting libvirt logs and VM XML definitions. Each objective is practical: installing packages and enabling libvirtd ensures the host is ready; building a virt-install command lets you reproduce VM creation; virsh commands let you script lifecycle automation. Troubleshooting skills reduce downtime by guiding you to journalctl and virsh dumpxml to find misconfigurations. These skills combine into a verified competency: a system administrator who can provision, connect, and diagnose KVM virtual machines confidently.

This second objectives slide expands the hands-on skills you'll practice. You will create a VM from an ISO or network location using virt-install with options for R A M, vcpus, disk path and format, and network bridge selection. You will practice connecting to the VM with virt-viewer for graphical setup and with virsh console for headless installs using serial parameters. You will also practice reading and interpreting virsh output and libvirt XML so you can confirm correct settings and recover from mistakes. Additionally, you will learn to choose qcow2 for flexible snapshots and smaller file sizes, and when to preserve disk images versus undefining definitions. Each objective explains why it matters: repeatable commands enable automation, the serial console lets you fix boot-time issues, and logs give a reliable path to troubleshooting. Complete these exercises to turn conceptual knowledge into repeatable system administration practice.

KVM and QEMU work together to provide full virtualization on Linux. KVM is the kernel module that exposes hardware virtualization extensions to guests, enabling near-native performance by allowing the guest C P U to run directly on the host C P U when possible. QEMU complements KVM by emulating devices and handling input and output, such as virtual disks, network interfaces, and display devices. Together they form a complete stack: KVM supplies the low-level C P U virtualization, and QEMU supplies machine emulation and device models. A concrete example is a Linux host with Intel VT-x: KVM will create virtual CPUs leveraging VT-x, and QEMU will present a virtual disk in qcow2 format and emulate a network card attached to a libvirt-managed bridge. A common misconception is treating them as interchangeable: they are separate layers — disabling QEMU removes device emulation but not the kernel hypervisor support, while missing KVM prevents hardware acceleration and forces full software emulation with poor performance. Key practice: when validating your virtualization setup, confirm the libvirtd service is running and that qemu-kvm packages are installed. That ensures both layers are present to create performant and fully featured VMs. Takeaway: think of KVM as the fast engine and QEMU as the dashboard and peripherals; both are needed for production virtual machines.

Before creating VMs you must install the necessary packages and enable the libvirt daemon. On Red Hat-based distributions, the canonical package set includes qemu-kvm, libvirt-daemon-kvm, libvirt-client, virt-install, and virt-viewer. Installing these packages brings the kernel module, the userland tools, the virt-install command and a graphical viewer for connecting to VMs. After installation, enable and start the libvirtd service so the daemon is active across reboots. Adding your user to the libvirt group removes the need to run virsh with sudo, which makes repeated administration easier and reduces accidental elevated commands. A concrete command sequence is shown in the lab: use dnf to install the packages, systemctl to enable and start libvirtd, and usermod with newgrp to apply group membership without logging out. A common mistake is forgetting to start libvirtd after install or skipping the newgrp step; without the daemon you cannot create or list domains, and without group membership you may get permission errors. After these steps run virsh list --all to confirm libvirt is reachable. That verifies the host is ready for VM creation. Install and enable libvirt and KVM packages means install qemu-kvm, libvirt-daemon-kvm, virt-install, and virt-viewer, enable libvirtd, and add your user to libvirt for permissioned management.. In practical terms, prepare the host so you can create and manage vms. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The virt-install command is the primary CLI to define and start virtual machines via libvirt. It accepts options for name, R A M, vCPU count, disk specification, OS variant, network, graphics, installation source, and extra arguments. For example, --name sets the VM identifier used by virsh and the image path; --R A M expects megabytes and --vcpus sets C P U count. The --disk option is flexible: path, size, and format can be set, and qcow2 is a common format because it supports copy-on-write snapshots. Use --os-variant to let virt-install pick tuned defaults for a particular guest operating system. The network option can bind to virbr0 or another bridge, which controls whether the VM is NATed or directly bridged. Graphics may be vnc or spice; for headless installs choose console parameters with --extra-args to enable serial installs. A misconception is that virt-install will always start a graphical console; in many test or server environments you'll want --noautoconsole and to use virt-viewer or virsh console instead. Understanding each flag makes it straightforward to build repeatable, automated VM creation commands for labs and production.

Let's walk through a concrete virt-install invocation and explain each piece as you would use it in a lab. The example creates a VM named my-web-server with 2 vCPUs, 2GB of R A M, and a 20GB qcow2 disk. It uses an rhel8.0 os-variant for tuned defaults, connects the VM to virbr0 so the guest has NAT networking, and enables VNC graphics for installation. The --location option points to an ISO image, and --extra-args sets a serial console so you can perform headless installs when needed. The --noautoconsole flag prevents virt-install from hijacking your terminal and leaves console connections to virt-viewer or virsh console. Practice building this command by changing --R A M and --vcpus to provision different sizes, and by swapping the disk path to a dedicated LVM volume for production workloads. virsh is the essential command-line tool for operating libvirt-managed virtual machines. It is used to list VMs, control their power state, and remove definitions when needed. Commonly used commands include virsh list --all to show all domains, virsh start to power a domain on, and virsh shutdown to request a graceful shutdown using ACPI. When a VM becomes unresponsive you can force power off with virsh destroy, but this is equivalent to unplugging power and can cause data loss. Use virsh suspend and virsh resume to pause and continue a VM's execution, which is useful for short maintenance. Removing a VM's libvirt definition is accomplished with virsh undefine; note that undefine removes the XML definition but leaves disk images on disk unless additional flags are used. For example, a safe recovery workflow is to run virsh destroy only if shutdown fails, then virsh undefine if you intend to re-create a fresh definition while keeping the image for analysis. A misconception is treating destroy as a delete; it does not remove disk files. Always back up disk images before destructive operations. Practice these commands so you can script lifecycle actions reliably during an LFCE exam or in production automation.

Access to a VM can be graphical or serial. virt-viewer provides a graphical window to a VM's console when you create VNC or Spice graphics; it is useful during installations and for desktops. To open a VM's graphical console run virt-viewer followed by the domain name. For headless servers, use a serial console configured via --extra-args in virt-install, which allows virsh console to attach to the guest's serial tty. The serial console is indispensable for servers without a desktop environment and for diagnosing early boot issues like kernel or init failures. A concrete example is adding --extra-args "console=ttyS0,115200n8 serial" to your virt-install command and then connecting with virsh console mytestvm to interact directly with the guest's installation or recovery shell. A common misconception is that virt-viewer or VNC is always available; many production hosts are strictly headless, so planning for serial access avoids being locked out. Always ensure your guest’s bootloader and kernel are configured to output to the serial device when you rely on virsh console. Closing question: which access method will you prioritize for a production headless server and why?

Choosing a disk format for VM images affects flexibility and operational behavior. qcow2, QEMU's Copy-On-Write format, is popular because it supports snapshots and usually consumes less space than an equivalent raw image due to its thin-provisioning nature. That makes qcow2 ideal for test environments and snapshots during upgrades. However, for high-performance production workloads administrators sometimes prefer block devices on LVM or raw images on dedicated storage to reduce overhead and simplify backup strategies. The virt-install --disk option lets you specify path, size, and format so you can choose qcow2 for flexibility or a raw path for performance. A key practical point is to always back up VM disk images before destructive operations like undefine or manual file deletion. In production, using LVM volumes or dedicated storage backends also helps with snapshot management and integration with storage platform features. A common misconception is that qcow2 is always slower; while there is an overhead compared to raw images, the operational advantages of snapshots and space savings often outweigh that cost for many use cases. Decide based on your workload and backup strategy.

libvirt typically provides a default virtual network called virbr0 that offers NAT-based connectivity for guests. This is useful for quickly giving VMs outbound network access without manually configuring bridges or host networking. Virbr0 is convenient for labs and for hosts where direct bridged access is not required. However, for production scenarios where a guest needs to be reachable from the same network as the host, administrators create a custom bridge tied to a physical interface and attach the VM directly to that bridge. The virt-install --network bridge=virbr0 flag attaches the VM to the default NAT network; to attach a custom bridge use the bridge name of your choice. A frequent pitfall is expecting virbr0 to provide incoming connections without additional NAT or port-forward rules — it does not expose guest services by default to the broader LAN. For production VMs that must serve traffic directly, plan for a bridged network or configure proper firewall and forwarding rules. Understanding the difference between NAT and bridged networking prevents connectivity surprises after VM provisioning. When virt-install or virsh operations fail, start with the error messages and then inspect two reliable sources: virsh dumpxml for the VM's configuration and journalctl -u libvirtd for daemon logs. If virt-install reports an ISO path error, verify that the path exists and is readable by libvirt. If a VM won't start, virsh dumpxml shows disks and network settings that can reveal misconfigured paths or missing devices. The libvirtd journal often contains permission or registration errors from qemu connecting to libvirt. For network failures, confirm your target bridge exists and that the host firewall is not blocking traffic. A recommended safe recovery is to avoid destructive commands until you have a backup: perform virsh shutdown first, then virsh destroy only if shutdown fails, and use virsh undefine only when you explicitly want to remove the definition and understand that disks remain unless you delete them. Always back up disk images before rm or destructive operations. A common misconception is that virsh destroy and undefine delete images; they do not, and administrators should treat disk removal as a separate, intentional step. Following this diagnostic path will minimize downtime and preserve data for analysis.

Keep these core ideas in mind as you practice. First, KVM and QEMU are distinct but complementary: KVM enables kernel-level virtualization while QEMU provides device emulation and input and output handling. Third, virsh is the operational tool for listing domains, starting, shutting down, suspending, and undefining VMs; always inspect virsh dumpxml and libvirt logs when troubleshooting.
